forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bassetlaw's forecast moves from £2.231m surplus to £2.769m cumulative gap by March 2030
news_drafts.lead:
Bassetlaw District Council's Cabinet has been given an updated medium-term financial plan (MTFP, the council's forecast of spending against income over the next few years) showing a cumulative budget gap of £2.769m by March 2030. In February 2026 the same forecast showed a cumulative surplus of £2.231m through to March 2029, a swing of about £5m.

The council attributes the change to updated funding assumptions, confirmed after the government's three-year Local Government Finance Settlement. The papers do not break the £5m down further.

The council plans to manage the gap in three ways. It will draw on earmarked reserves (money set aside for a named purpose): £1.650m in 2026/27, then £481,000 and £1.161m in the following two years. It will identify further savings and efficiency measures through future budget processes, though the papers do not put a figure on these. And it expects some help from the outcome of future government Spending Reviews. For 2029/30 the plan is to use the Financial Resilience Reserve, set up for this purpose, alongside additional savings. The council says relying on reserves to balance the budget carries inherent risks and is not sustainable in the long term.

findings.paper_title: 8b Finance and Performance Monitoring Q2 2026-27 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Bassetlaw's balance sheet resilience measures show an overall positive direction of travel over 2023/24 to 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says the strongest improvements are in usable reserves, general fund balances, pension liabilities, capital reserves and the relationship between borrowing and available resources. It notes some measures remain under monitoring, mainly accounting balances, liquidity and treasury indicators.
findings.matters: A three-year balance sheet assessment is the kind of evidence lenders and peer finance officers use to judge a council's resilience, including the parts the paper says still need watching.
findings.quote: shows an overall positive direction of travel

findings.paper_title: 8b Finance and Performance Monitoring Q2 2026-27 - Cabinet
findings.headline: The Priory Centre redevelopment's main construction phase has started, with fit-out expected to take 12 months against a March 2028 funding deadline.
findings.detail: The paper says demolition is complete and the main construction phase has commenced under a revised delivery programme. It says the Local Regeneration Fund changes remove rigid delivery timescales and allow underspend to be reallocated from former LUF2 and Levelling Up Partnership projects.
findings.matters: A scheme with a fixed funding deadline and a 12-month build window is an example of how councils are timing capital delivery against regeneration funding conditions.
findings.figures: March 2028 revised funding deadline; 12 months construction and fit-out
findings.quote: this phase and fit out is expected to take 12 months which fits in with the revised funding

findings.paper_title: 8b Finance and Performance Monitoring Q2 2026-27 - Cabinet
findings.headline: The 2026/27 capital programme is revised to £80.5m at 30 September 2026, from £84.5m at 30 June after £4.0m of Q2 budget movements.
findings.detail: The paper reports a total live programme of £145.7m across 2026/27 and later years, with borrowing funding 46% of the total. Members are asked to approve a further £0.7m increase in proposed budget movements, of which £0.1m is pending officer decisions.
findings.matters: Borrowing making up 46% of the programme, and a live budget that has moved down in-year, are the figures a lender and a finance director would track against the council's borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: £80.5m revised 2026/27 budget; £84.5m at 30 June 2026; £4.0m Q2 reduction; £145.7m total programme; £33.1m 2026/27 borrowing; 46% borrowing share of total; £0.7m proposed increase

findings.paper_title: 8b Finance and Performance Monitoring Q2 2026-27 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Neighbourhoods forecasts an £831k adverse variance, driven by agency costs, waste vehicle hire and trade waste income shortfalls.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the variance mainly to agency costs in Waste Management and Transport, with a further £120k on collection vehicle hire and route software and underachieved trade waste and garden waste income. Service delivery options to reduce agency reliance are being progressed.
findings.matters: A large, multi-cause service overspend is the kind of pressure peer finance officers will be comparing against their own waste and transport budgets.
findings.figures: £831k forecast adverse variance; £347k at Q1; £123k Waste Management agency; £99k Transport agency; £120k vehicle hire and route software; £106k trade waste income shortfall; £63k garden waste subscriptions shortfall
findings.quote: Neighbourhoods - A £831k adverse variance is forecast.

findings.paper_title: 8b Finance and Performance Monitoring Q2 2026-27 - Cabinet
findings.headline: Employee costs are forecast at a £257k adverse variance, as vacancy underspends no longer cover the £713k vacancy factor and agency costs.
findings.detail: The paper says the vacancy factor will not be met, and that the increase in agency costs and the NJC pay award at 3.3% (0.3% above the Q1 assumption) have worsened the position. People and Transformation's £171k adverse variance is linked to staff healthcare contract costs and the apprenticeship levy.
findings.matters: A vacancy factor that is no longer being met is a common budget pressure, and the paper shows it as a specific, quantified shortfall against a stated factor.
findings.figures: £257k adverse employee cost variance; £148k worsened since Q1; £713k vacancy factor; £77k higher agency costs than Q1; 3.3% NJC pay award; £119k staff healthcare contract cost increase
findings.quote: The level of underspends relating to vacancies is no longer sufficient to cover the vacancy factor and the cost of agency.
